params.textField: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone mechanism can be thought of as the panic button for increasing blood pressure as much as possible. It orchestrates all of our individual mechanisms that are designed to increase blood pressure, and begins by simply by releasing one enzyme. When the kidneys sense a decrease in *blood pressure* or an increase in *sympathetic nervous system stimulation* at the level of the glomerulus, there is a release of the enzyme *renin*, which changes *angiotensinogen* to angiotensin I. When angiotensin 1 goes through the lungs, it is cleaved by an enzyme called *angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE)* to form *angiotensin II*, which is a potent hormone that affects many organs. For instance, angiotensin II has direct *vasoconstricting* actions on the peripheral blood vessels, increases the release of *ADH* the water saver from the posterior pituitary gland and *aldosterone* the salt saver from the adrenal cortex. Our antihypertensive medications attempt to stop this cascade at various points. For instance, *ACE inhibitors* block the enzyme in the lungs that changes angiotensin I to angiotensin II and *Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBS)* block the angiotensin II receptors at the various organs.

ACE inhibitors act as a type of diuretic, excreting more salt and water from the system, but are not considered diuretics because they have many more actions than diuresis.

answers.text: Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBS) like candesartan and other …sartan drugs block the angiotensin II receptors at multiple sites, thereby resulting in at least 5 different ways in which blood pressure is decreased. They ultimately decrease the release of ADH, the water saver, decrease the release of aldosterone, the salt saver, and decrease the direct vasoconstriction effect normally caused by angiotensin II (as well as other ways).
Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBS) increase potassium levels and are often combined with a diuretic such as hydrochlorothiazide which excretes more potassium.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: NO, this statement is incorrect. The incidence of cough in clients taking candesartan is only about 1-2% and the origin of the cough is not known. Many clients who were taken off ACE inhibitors think that candesartan is causing a cough because the ACE inhibitor-induced cough lasts as long as 3 months.

answers.text: Candesartan can cause a chronic dry cough in 10% of patients, and that cough is similar to that caused by ACE inhibitors.
